newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: BP unit to invest $600 mln in Colombia in 1997.
newsitem.headline: BP unit to invest $600 mln in Colombia in 1997.

text.p: British Petroleum Co Plc's local subsidiary will be looking to make net investments of about $600 million in its Colombian oil operations in 1997, its executive director John Doust said on Thursday.
BP Exploration (Company) Ltd this year pushed its total net investment in Colombia since arriving in 1989 to $2 billion -- maintaining its position as the country's single largest foreign investor.
BP's investment in Colombia now accounts for 12 percent of its total worldwide, Doust said.
In a speech to journalists, Doust said BP Exploration had exported 41 million barrels of crude oil drawn from the Cusiana- Cupiagua fields in Colombia's eastern plains region in 1996.
The average rate of production at Cusiana-Cupiagua currently stands at almost 175,000 barrels a day. Accumulated production from the field was 114 million barrels to the end of November.

Phase Two of the development is due for completion by the end of 1997 by which time production should have risen to 500,000 barrels a day, Doust said. The mid-year production target is 320,000 barrrels a day.

Phase Two of the project will cost an estimated $4 billion, Doust said, but some of those costs will be split with its partners Total, Triton and its associate Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol. The cost also includes a major new pipeline, already under construction, which will run from BP's operations in northeastern Casanare province to the Caribbean coast oil terminal at Covenas.

Doust said the pipeline project was technically challenging, "as difficult as the TransAlaska pipeline". The new 500 mile (800 km) Colombian pipeline has to cross mountain ranges as high as 10,000 feet with gradients as steep as 60 and 70 percent.

Attacks by leftist guerrillas are another frequent problem in Colombia. The pipeline is being built with a self-sealing mechanism which will enable parts of the pipeline to be shut off and prevent major spillages in the event of rebels blasting it, Doust explained.

The burden of major new financial commitments to the Cusiana-Cupiagua field have been partially offset by a reduction in drilling times and costs through 1996. Colombia is known for its often difficult drilling conditions -- a problem BP is also encountering in its Piedemonte field also in the eastern plains zone.

"A significant reduction in costs and drilling time has been achieved in Cupiagua and (this) translated into significant savings for Ecopetrol and our partners. It was achieved by technology transfer and the experience of foreign engineers and Colombian professionals trained to face the industry's challenge," Doust said.

In addition to stepping up production and exports in 1997, BP will be looking to make inroads into the domestic natural gas market. It has already entered memorandums of understanding with a number of companies to sell 500 cubic gigafeet of natural gas.
BP is also carrying out a joint feasibility study to look at the construction of a thermal power plant in Casanare of 1,000 megawatts, Doust said.
